newsitem.title: ICELAND: Weather foils bids to predict Icelandic flood.
newsitem.headline: Weather foils bids to predict Icelandic flood.

text.p: A tower of grey-white steam hung over Europe's largest glacier on Wednesday, in stark relief against the clear blue sky as a volcanic eruption under the ice cap raged on unabated.
A choking sulphurous odour filled a light aircraft carrying scientists over the scene. At the base of the column, smoke billowed out steadily like fungus growing in a time-compressed film sequence.
The volcano under the Vatnajokull glacier has been erupting for eight days, steadily melting the ice cap. The resulting melt water has filled the Grimsvotn subglacial lake to the brim.
The ice could lift at any time, leaving the waters to flood down to the black sand plains at the foot of the glacier.
Wednesday saw a break in four days of atrocious weather, and scientists were able to fly over the meringue-like glacier to try to assess when the floods might arrive.
But low cloud around the eight km (five mile) fissure in the ice foiled attempts on Wednesday to judge how close the lake was to overflowing.
"We could see that the water level in the lake had risen, but we were unable to make accurate measurements," Bryndis Brandsdottir, seismologist at the University of Iceland, told Reuters.
"The seismic tremors from the eruptions remain steady. We are still waiting for the flood," she added.
The only visual sign of the furious activity deep below Vatnajokull is the steam column rising from the fissure that opened as the eruption tore its way through the ice cap over a week ago.

Most of the ash from the eruption has been contained in the ice, forming a 200 metre (yard) high slope reminiscent of a slag heap at the head of a coal mine, but what little has escaped has formed a dirty smudge on the otherwise pure white surface.
It is estimated the water from the brimming lake will surge out in torrents of up to 25 metres per second, flooding the surrounding black sand plain, uninhabitated but for sheep.

The area, declared an emergency zone, remains deserted except for the occasional group of journalists and government workers trying to protect the country's one coastal ring road, which passes through a small settlement southwest of the glacier, from the flood.
Government estimates put the cost of the expected flood in a worst-case scenario at 1.5 billion Icelandic crowns ($22 million), assuming all the bridges, roads, power lines in the area are wiped out.
But the actual cost to public finances would be limited. Most of the cost would be borne by an insurance fund set up by the government after a massive volcanic eruption in 1973.
"We have a long history of natural disasters, and have prepared for them with the fund," Olafur Davidsson, secretary general in the prime minister's office told Reuters.
"We see this very much as a part of living in this country. Disasters are something we are always aware of and something we must prepare for."
